steps.caption: Clothes for the top half of your body and for going out. A jumper is warm, and a raincoat keeps you dry in the rain. A suit is a jacket with matching trousers, and people often wear a tie with it.
Clothes for your legs or your whole body. Jeans are trousers made of denim. You wear a tracksuit for sport, a swimming costume at the pool and a costume at a fancy dress party.
Shoes and accessories. Trainers are sports shoes, sandals are open shoes for summer and boots cover your feet and ankles. A scarf keeps your neck warm, and you carry your things in a handbag.
Jewellery is rings, earrings, bracelets and chains. Jewellery is uncountable: we say «a lot of jewellery», not «jewelleries».
An outfit is a set of clothes that you wear together. To talk about clothes in the past, use wore, the past of wear: «She wore a long blue dress and sandals.»
To say what someone has on now, use is wearing: «He's wearing a tracksuit and trainers.» A tracksuit and trainers are his outfit today.
Useful phrases in a clothes shop. «Try on» means put clothes on in the shop to see if they are the right size.

Can I try them on, please?

steps.caption: Parts of clothes: a shirt has buttons, a collar round the neck and two sleeves for your arms. A T-shirt has short sleeves and a jumper has long sleeves.
Patterns: a striped shirt has stripes, a spotted dress has spots and a patterned skirt has a pattern, for example flowers. A plain T-shirt has no spots and no stripes.

To say what clothes are made of, use «It's made of …»: «My scarf is made of wool.» Natural materials come from plants and animals. Artificial (synthetic) materials are made in factories. Denim is made from cotton.
Synthetic fleece is made from plastic. When we wash it, very small pieces of plastic go into the water, so it can pollute rivers and the sea.
People like artificial textiles because they are cheaper than natural ones. Smart textiles are new materials that can change: for example, they can change colour.
Adjectives to describe clothes and people. Casual clothes are for relaxing; smart clothes are for special days.
Put the describing words in this order: opinion, pattern, material, then the clothes: «a comfortable striped cotton T-shirt».

topics.name: Comparing: Adjectives, Adverbs and as … as

steps.caption: To compare two things, short adjectives add -er + than. Long adjectives use more + adjective + than. Good and bad are irregular.
Big ends in one vowel and one consonant, so we double the g: big → bigger than. «My bag is bigger than yours.»
Long adjectives don't add -er. Use more + adjective + than: «This jumper is more colourful than that one.»
An adverb of manner tells us how we do something. Most are adjective + -ly: «She writes neatly.» Good → well and fast → fast are irregular: «He plays well. She runs fast.»
To compare how people do things, use more + adverb + than: «Ana writes more neatly than me.» Well → better and fast → faster: «Tom swims faster than Leo.»
as + adjective or adverb + as means the same (equal): «He's as tall as Krish.» «Max plays the guitar as well as Krish.»
not as + adjective + as means less: «Her new schoolbag is not as big as her old one.» «Ben isn't as brave as Frankie» means Frankie is braver than Ben.

questions.explanation: Big is a short adjective, so we add -er + than. It ends in one vowel and one consonant, so the g doubles: bigger.

questions.explanation: Comfortable is a long adjective, so we use more + adjective + than: more comfortable than.

questions.explanation: Bad is irregular: bad → worse than.

questions.prompt: Please write ___. I can't read your homework!
questions.explanation: We need an adverb to say how you write. Neat is an adjective; the adverb is neat + -ly: neatly.

questions.prompt: Leo is a good swimmer. He swims very ___.
questions.explanation: Good is an adjective. Its adverb is irregular: good → well. He swims well.

questions.prompt: Max is 1.40 m tall and Krish is 1.40 m tall. Max is ___ Krish.
questions.explanation: They are the same height, so we use as + adjective + as: Max is as tall as Krish.

questions.prompt: Lily's jumper has red, yellow, green and blue stripes. It's ___ than mine.
questions.explanation: Colourful is a long adjective, so we use more + adjective + than: more colourful than.

questions.prompt: A car goes ___ than a bike.
questions.explanation: Fast is irregular: the adverb is fast, and the comparative is faster than.

questions.prompt: Her new schoolbag is not as ___ as her old one. The old one was bigger.
questions.explanation: After not as … as we use the normal adjective: not as big as. It means the new bag is smaller.

questions.prompt: Mia checks every answer. She does her homework ___ than her brother.
questions.explanation: We need an adverb to say how she does her homework. Carefully ends in -ly, so we use more carefully than.

steps.caption: We can use the present simple to talk about the future when it is a timetable or a schedule: «The bus leaves in five minutes.»
Buses, trains, flights, shows and classes happen at fixed times, so we use the present simple for them.

tiles.label: The bus leaves in five minutes.
The fashion show starts at one o'clock tomorrow.
The flight arrives in Prague at 10 a.m.

steps.caption: With he, she, it or one thing, add -s or -es to the verb: the show starts, the bus leaves, the party finishes. With plural subjects there is no -s: «The models arrive at ten.»
Questions use does or do + the base verb, with no -s: «What time does the flight leave? When does the party start? What days do they have parties?»
rewrite: What time does the flight leave?

steps.caption: Negatives use doesn't or don't + the base verb: «The party doesn't start at seven.» «The shops don't open on Sundays.»
Pronunciation tip: the s at the end of plural nouns or he, she and it verbs often sounds like /z/: leaves, arrives.
